Moderator: 
Ladies and gentlemen, good day, and welcome to the Tata Consumer Products Q2 FY27 
Earnings Conference Call. As a reminder, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode 
and there will be an opportunity for you to ask questions after the presentation concludes. 
Should you need assistance during this conference, please signal an operator by pressing star 
then zero on your touchtone phone. Please note that this conference is being recorded. 
 
I now hand the conference over to Ms. Nidhi Verma, Head of Investor Relations and Corporate 
Communications. Thank you, and over to you. 
Nidhi Verma: 
Thank you. Thank you so much, everyone, for joining us today. We announced our Q2 FY27 
results earlier in the evening. I hope you've had a chance to go through the materials. As usual, 
I am joined by Mr. Sunil D'Souza, Managing Director and CEO; Mr. Ashish Goenka, Group 
CFO; and Mr. Ajit Krishnakumar, Executive Director and COO. In terms of the format, we'll 
walk you through key business updates for the first 20 minutes or so, and then we will open the 
floor for Q&A. 
 
So with that, I just want to quickly draw your attention to the disclaimer statement, which is on 
your screen. With that, I'll hand it over to Sunil. 
Sunil D'Souza: 
Thanks, Nidhi. So, in summary, we grew top line 14% with UVG of 11% in the India business. 
Salt was another strong quarter of 9% volume and 15% revenue. India tea volumes were flat. 
Revenue was marginally lower year-on-year. Growth businesses had another strong quarter. 
Sampann was up 57%. Ready-to-Drink is now strongly back on the growth trajectory with 
47%. 
 
Capital Foods and Organic India were up 15%, but the domestic business was very strong 
because international was impacted by shipping disruptions as well as the Mundra Port issue in 
early September. International business grew 7% in constant currency was negative 2%, but 
had a very, very strong margin delivery. 
 
Non-branded grew 12%, 9% in constant currency. Consolidated EBITDA was up 18%, with 
margins expanding 40 bps to bring EBITDA margin to 14%. Starbucks had probably one of 
their strongest quarters ever, revenue growing 15% and with strong same-store sales growth. I 
think now they have 5 or 6 successive quarters of positive same-store sales growth and very 
strong results. 
 
So India Salt crossed -- was close to INR1,100 crores. It's coming to touching distance of India 
Tea/Coffee now, up 15%. India Tea/Coffee largely impacted by weather, a little bit of price 
increases in tea and a little bit of a hangover of the disruptions in Q1, of the LPG issues, was 
down 1%. Growth businesses up 40% to close to INR1,400 crores, continue to be now 
powering ahead of our salt and tea-coffee businesses. International close to INR1,300 crores, 
up 7%, non-branded up 12% and consolidated up 14%. Constant currency was 11%. 
 
In terms of first half, India Salt up 11%. India tea and coffee, if you remember, the first quarter 
was minus 4% on revenue. This quarter was minus 1%. So overall, minus 3% as you've taken 
up prices. Growth businesses up 43%, international up 11%; non-branded up 3% and

consolidated at close to INR11,000 crores. The beauty of the portfolio, if you look at it, salt, 
tea-coffee, growth, international, now we've got 4 strong legs on the TCPL stool. 
 
In terms of financial performance, revenue up 14%, EBITDA up 18%, profit before taxes up 
21% and net profit at INR470 crores, growing 16%. EPS of 4.75. And as we said, if we 
amortize -- because we amortize certain brands, if I take that off, our adjusted EPS is 5.18. For 
the first half, revenue up 13%, EBITDA 18%, profit before tax 24%, net profit up 22%, 
adjusted EPS of 9.85. 
 
In terms of the businesses, overall, our A&P-to-Sales for the quarter was 5.5% and for the -- 
first half was 5.8%. Just a perspective here is we've reclassified visibility separately and A&P 
separately. That's why this number you will see separately. Visibility is knocked off from 
revenue up top. In the ballpark, we are in the same number of about 6.3% to 6.5% in total 
A&P-to-Sales. 
 
Growth businesses up 40%, now contribute to 38% of India business. We've started our 
significant transformational journey with AI with about 1,600/ 1,700 salesmen, which we have 
on date as of now with an objective by December to reach 100% of our salespeople operating. 
There is a personalized AI sales companion guiding the salesmen outlet by outlet, SKU by 
SKU on what exactly to do. 
 
And where the salesman misses the outlet, there is a voice agent, which does call up the 
retailer and does the ordering process. The sales executive gets a concise summary of what 
exactly the DSR did at every single outlet with a follow-up on what coaching is needed out 
there. That's on the sales front. 
 
On the operations front, we have started deploying -- we've deployed AI to recognize close to 
120 different types of leaves that come into the factory so that we qualify quality and pricing 
of the leaf, per se, of stuff entering into the factory. In the Himalayan factory, we've got AI 
starting to do online bottle inspection. Around the corner, we've got a history of tea in terms of 
temperature, rainfall, crop price, etcetera. 
 
We are going to use that to start guiding our procurement team on when to buy, at what price 
to buy. We've already started automation with invoice validation and payment. We've got an 
engine running at the back end online on consumer insights. We are feeding both to our R&D 
team as well as our marketing innovation. 
 
We've started trade spend optimizer as a pilot, which we rolled out for tea for the entire 
country starting this month, and we have started to see substantial savings. And apart from 
that, we are looking at experimenting with AI calling for retailers where we can drop 
frequency to visits to outlets which order less than two times a month. 
 
So, we move from a weekly to a fortnightly frequency with the alternate week AI agent calling 
in to make sure no order is missed. So these are a few examples of what is already in play. We 
will be continuing to make sure that we have robust business cases as we expand AI across the 
enterprise.

We had 22 new product launches in Q2, total 36 for the first half, as I said, focused on 
differentiated propositions in health and wellness, convenience and premiumization. In terms 
of businesses, as I mentioned, volume overall was flat for tea and coffee, revenue was minus 
1%. But just as a perspective, Q1 was volume plus 2%, value minus 4%. 
 
As we took graduated calibrated price increases in tea, we've come to a flat volume and 
revenue minus 1%. So from a minus -- from a 6 percentage difference, volume value, we are 
1% here. And as we've continued taking graduated price increases, we expect the equation to 
start turning value greater than volume starting this quarter. 
 
Next. Salt, we took a price increase of about 6%. We moved from INR30 to INR32 for the 
orange bag in May. October first week, we moved another Rs. 2. So the INR32 has become 
INR34. But this is reported before that happened. So volume was up 9%, revenue was plus 
15%. Value-added and premium salts continue to deliver 2x the growth of the base salt 
business, continue to expand their contribution to the portfolio. 
 
Sampann, strong quarter, revenue up 57%, driven by strong volume growth as well. Dry fruits 
and cold-pressed oil now combined ARR of INR1,000 crores plus, and we will continue to 
expand the portfolio with margin expansion as we go forward. RTD, having reset the entire 
business, has now started delivering strong results, volume up 34%, revenue up 47%. Growth 
remained broad-based across the portfolio, both with the base business as well as innovation 
driving top lines. 
 
Capital Foods and Organic India, overall, 18% in Capital Foods, 9% in Organic India. 
Domestic business was strong. If I put both together, 24% top line growth. As I said, this 
quarter, the disruption in shipping and I think about 10 to 12 days of disruption at the Mundra 
port was the prime reason for international not coming to the party completely. But we firmly 
believe that having reset the go-to-market in India, Capital Foods and Organic India are on a 
strong growth wicket. 
 
International, overall, negative 2% in constant currency, lapping a high base, but overall 
revenue of 7%. The U.K. was impacted by the continued heat wave for the quarter. The good 
news is the weather has turned, and I do think U.K. is going to come back strongly because 
share continued to hold out. Revenue declined 8% in the U.K., but U.S. business grew 4%, 
expanded margins with 6% constant currency growth in coffee. Canada continued their strong 
growth with 8% constant currency and South Africa also had a very strong quarter. 
 
Non-branded business grew 9% on an elevated base of last year. Robusta and Arabica prices 
continue to soften, impacting realizations, but margins continue to be healthy for the 
plantations business as well. The soluble volume grew 21% as we executed strongly both 
operationally and made sure that deliveries kept pace. 
 
Starbucks, as I mentioned, had a very strong quarter. It's a fifth successive quarter of same-
store sales growth, 15% top line. We had calibrated store openings to get our new business 
model in place. More or less, I think we've got it, and we've seen strong growth in traffic as

Ashish Goenka:

point margin expansion and adjusted EPS grew at 17%. In terms of first half, the growth has 
been at 13%. Again, I think overall EBITDA growth was ahead of top line at 18% and then 
that led to a 60-basis point margin expansion for the first half. Our adjusted EPS again grew 
ahead of EBITDA growth at 21%, coming at INR9.85. 
 
Looking at segments. India for the quarter, there was a bit of a contraction of the margin, 
largely on account of the inflationary pressures that we are seeing on tea and salt. Having said 
that, of course, we have taken calibrated pricing, which should start from quarter 3. 
 
Both international and non-branded had a very substantial improvement in profitability and 
leading to an overall improvement in segment margins by 50 basis points. The same is 
reflected at a first half level, where all 3 segments have actually improved on profitability 
across India, international and non-branded, leading to an overall 100 basis points in segment 
margin overall. 
 
That's pretty much the summary of financials. I think I'll hand back to Nidhi now for anchoring 
the Q&A.

Moderator, maybe we can go to the Q&A queue to take the questions.

Certainly. Thank you very much. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Our 
first question comes from the line of Mihir Shah with Nomura. 
Mihir Shah: 
Congrats on a great set of numbers. My first question is actually on tea. Sir, if you can just talk 
about is the procurement for the year largely done in tea? What is the level of inflation that you 
are seeing on a Y-o-Y basis? And can you share the quantum of price increase that you're 
putting through? We are seeing some kind of price increase in the market. So that's question 
number one. 
Sunil D'Souza: 
So overall, see, broadly, while tea volumes have been flattish, volumes value has been flattish, 
market share is stable. So there's -- it's not that things have moved. It's overall industry has 
been soft. I think if I look at overall third-party numbers, it's about negative 6% is what the 
number shows. So in that perspective, I think we are in a not too bad space. 
 
We have taken pricing roughly, I would say, between Q1 to now, you would have seen roughly 
around 8% to 10% pricing, which is in line with the inflation that we've seen in tea. While the 
initial bump in the Q1, Q2 was about 7% to 8%. Right now, if you look on a week-to-week 
basis, it's broadly in the 2% to 3%.

Sunil D'Souza: 
See, we had guided for 50 to 70 bps expansion when we started off the year. We've seen

INR30 to INR32, INR32 to INR34. So as we've seen any bit of pressure on costs, we've 
translated into price to make sure we maintain volume. We remain aggressively focused on 
expanding margins for the year. 
Mihir Shah: 
Understood. Secondly, on Sampann, another very strong quarter. Can you share with the quick 
commerce expanding its dark stores reach in Tier 2, are the products getting well accepted 
there? Are you seeing repeat purchases? Or is it too soon there? And what subcategories we 
saw that oils and dry fruits have already crossed INR1,000 crores. So what subcategories are 
doing well and have reached a sizable contribution? And on the flip side, which are the ones 
that are not doing as per your expectations? 
Sunil D'Souza: 
So the good news is I don't think there are any of the new launches which are not doing the 
expectations. Like I've said earlier, in our innovation funnel, if the product doesn't deliver in 
the first 6 months, then we take a call on it, maximum life support for 3 more months or else 
out, right? That's the only way you can sustain growth on the innovation platform. That's 
number one. 
 
Number 2, in terms of quick commerce, I think one leading player declared their results last 
quarter. And our growth in quick commerce is almost in the same ballpark. So we are growing 
with the quick commerce players as they're expanding dark stores, number two. 
 
Number 3 is which categories are doing well with quick commerce. Actually speaking, if you 
look at it, Sampann across the portfolio all our categories are either mostly Number 1 or a few 
of them are Number 2 positions across platforms. So from that perspective, I think the team 
has done a good job in playing with them as we expand. While dry fruits and cold-pressed oils 
ARR is now north of INR1,000 crores, the base categories of pulses, poha, makhana, all these 
things are also in the 30%-plus range as we go forward. 
 
So Sampann, I think, is on a very strong footing. The other good part is that, as I said, when we 
started off 5 years back, we were negative 5% margin. We are seeing margin expansion on a 
continuous basis, both as we build scale as well as layer on variants to make sure we drive 
margins along with top line. So this quarter also compared to the same quarter last year, I think 
we had at 270, 280 bps of expansion on margin on Sampann as well. 
Mihir Shah: 
Understood. Understood. Very clear. Sorry, Sunil, I'm just asking on margins again, just to be 
very clear because last year, in the second half, we had seen across businesses margins seeing 
an improvement and versus now it is on a higher base. So I wanted to get your clear

understanding on how should one think about margins on an overall consolidated basis for the 
second half? 
Sunil D'Souza: 
See, overall, whether it is for tea, where we now start hitting peak season in India or 
international, which was impacted by the heat wave and now winter has already started to set 
in strongly in the north. So we see no reasons why tea should not increase, number one. 
Number two, salt, we've already taken the price increases to put margins back in strong 
footing. 
 
For Capital Foods, Q3, Q4, our peak festival and offtake season. So, from every angle, we 
remain quite confident of continuing to deliver margin expansion quarter-on-quarter versus -- 
when I say quarter-on-quarter, it is -- you would have to take seasonality into account, so it is 
versus the same quarter last year. So despite the fact that we delivered higher margins in H2 
versus H1 last year, we remain confident of continuing to deliver that this year as well.

Our next question comes from the line of Abhineesh Roy with Nuvama.

Congrats on a good set of numbers. So my first question is on the AI slide and the advertising 
details which you gave out in the initial remarks. So first is, based on the AI, I think most 
companies currently are doing, are you seeing a cost advantage also? Or is it just a companion 
to the sales team? I understand the language bit. I understand that 1 week, the sales team need 
not go. 
 
Is there any real cost advantage till now or just more of a companion to the salesperson? That 
is first part to that slide. Second bit is more on the advertising and the visibility bit which you 
put for the India business. If I see salt is a smaller part of the business, tea and coffee is around 
10% bigger than salt business. 
 
And the growth business is again 10% broadly bigger than tea and coffee business. My 
question is from an overall publicity budget in terms of, say, visibility plus mass media 
advertising, what will be the broad split between these 3 business so we can understand that it 
is a bit related to the sales bit also, sales percentage also? 
Sunil D'Souza: 
Abhineesh, number one is visibility is not included in this A&P. And as quick commerce has 
continued to power ahead, we've continued to invest more behind visibility to make sure we 
drive penetration and market share in those channels, right? That's number one. 
 
Number two, to your question on AI, we firmly believe, yes, there will be a cost takeout using 
AI, but that will be par for the course for everyone. The real differentiator comes in how do 
you bump up your revenue lines with AI. So the AI pilots, which we ran gave us a distinct 
lines per call improvement in the DSR calls, and that is when we decided to scale it. So there is 
a top line improvement outlet by outlet because it is very, very targeted. There is a memory 
function and we're building our sales brain behind it. So that's number two. 
 
Number three, in terms of overall visibility spends, etcetera, we are more on Sampann than for 
tea and salt. That is because Sampann as a category is also skewed towards more online

modern trade businesses. And therefore, it is more of visibility shopper marketing spend that

Abhineesh Roy: 
Sure. My second question is on the salt business. Last 7, 8 quarters, salt business in India has 
seen very good volume growth. Q2, the 9% volume growth, is it because there was some 
upfront buying because price hikes are now happening or the local players because they don't 
have the same capability to arrange the energy sources in the current turmoil and energy usage

the volume growth in salt business?

So Abhineesh, I don't think it is volume upload because it's not that we have seen any 
slowdown even after we've taken the second round of price increase, but that is a point in time 
for now. I can't -- there might be an impact going forward, but I don't see that realistically 
happening. I think the entire work that the team has done on building equity, diversifying 
portfolio, getting in the value-added salt, like I said in one of the earlier calls, it's almost like a 
Udupi menu, right, in terms of the types of salt we can get. 
 
This quarter also, we launched Tata Salt Plus, which is a double purified solar salt variant in 
the market. So, from that perspective, nothing changes. We have consistently maintained -- our 
market share is now close to 40%, 38.8% -- sorry, 39.8%, 39.9%. 
 
So, we are growing market share as well. I don't think it is because there is a short supply in 
the market or there is an energy issue. It's just that the entire work the team has done on 
building the brand equity, distribution, portfolio expansion, I think all that is coming into play. 
We continue to guide salt for mid-single-digit volume, a couple of basis points of price, and 
that is what we remain committed to delivering. 
Abhineesh Roy: 
Last question. So, Capital Foods plus Organic India, 24% domestic growth, if you can give a 
split between the two? And could you elaborate on the Mundra strike's impact? Do you expect

So Abhineesh, I think Mundra, there was a port strike for roughly around 10 days. So shipping 
got disrupted a bit apart from the fact that now a lot of shipping is getting diverted instead of 
going through the Middle East, it's going all the way around. So that is what has impacted our 
international business overall. 
 
Now I don't -- there might be a minor shift that will happen. There will be some uplift because 
as we catch up that gap, there will be some uplift coming into this quarter. But overall, I would 
continue to expect 25% to 30% growth that we had guided for Capital Foods and Organic 
India going forward. 
 
Domestic, I think, like I said, having relaid the entire go-to-market by February this year, 
having proved that system works where we have salt, non-salt, we have core, noncore and then 
we have regular distributors. I think that has brought back immense amount of focus. And by

geography, test it out, works, scale it up quickly, then go to modern trade, etcetera. So, this e-

what has helped us.
